multiple-choice.prompt: Why can an icy road extend braking distance?

multiple-choice.prompt: What is the main design aim of a rigid occupant cell?

multiple-choice.prompt: Why compare a cushion and a concrete barrier by site?

options.text: They may slow, absorb or redirect differently depending on the hazard.

multiple-choice.prompt: Which statement about side-impact beams is justified?

multiple-choice.hint: Name the quantity, mechanism or assumption before choosing.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Time between detecting a hazard and beginning a response.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: The driver takes 1.2 s to start braking.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: reaction time: Time between detecting a hazard and beginning a response. Time interval, not distance.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Distance travelled during reaction time before braking.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: At 15 m/s for 1 s, the vehicle travels 15 m.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: reaction distance: Distance travelled during reaction time before braking. Excludes travel while braking.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: A condition that could cause harm.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: A pedestrian enters a crossing ahead.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: hazard: A condition that could cause harm. A hazard is not proof that harm occurred.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: The chance of harm under specified conditions.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: Low visibility may increase collision risk.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: risk: The chance of harm under specified conditions. Risk is not a certain outcome.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Reduced ability to perceive, judge or respond effectively.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: Fatigue delays a driver’s response.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: impairment: Reduced ability to perceive, judge or respond effectively. Not measured by one feeling alone.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Attention diverted from the driving task.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: Looking at a phone delays noticing a crossing.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: distraction: Attention diverted from the driving task. A distraction need not last long to matter.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Tiredness that can reduce attention and response.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: A long shift increases missed cues.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: fatigue: Tiredness that can reduce attention and response. Feeling stimulated does not erase it.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Blood alcohol concentration, a measured amount of alcohol in blood.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: A laboratory result reports a BAC for a particular time.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: BAC: Blood alcohol concentration, a measured amount of alcohol in blood. A workbook estimate is not a measurement.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Action or design that reduces the chance of an event.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: A clear warning before a sharp curve.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: prevention: Action or design that reduces the chance of an event. Different from reducing injury after impact.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Action or design that reduces severity when an event occurs.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: A roadside barrier changes the impact path.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: mitigation: Action or design that reduces severity when an event occurs. Does not guarantee prevention.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Seat component that supports the head in some impacts.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: A properly positioned restraint limits head-neck motion.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: head restraint: Seat component that supports the head in some impacts. It is not a braking device.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Checking and repairing equipment to keep it working.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: Inspecting tires and lights.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: maintenance: Checking and repairing equipment to keep it working. Does not replace safe decisions.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Total path length travelled, without direction.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: A winding trip covers 500 m.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: distance: Total path length travelled, without direction. Not the same as change in position.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Change in position with direction.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: The finish is 200 m east of the start.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: displacement: Change in position with direction. Can be zero after a round trip.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Rate of distance travelled.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: 300 km in 2 h averages 150 km/h.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: speed: Rate of distance travelled. Does not state direction.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Speed with direction of motion.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: 20 m/s east.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: velocity: Speed with direction of motion. Direction is essential.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Graph of distance against elapsed time.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: A plotted line rises as a runner moves.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: distance–time graph: Graph of distance against elapsed time. It is not a map of the path.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Left-to-right axis, used here for time.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: Time (s) is labeled below the graph.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: horizontal axis: Left-to-right axis, used here for time. Do not put distance there for this task.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Vertical change divided by horizontal change.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: 10 m rise over 5 s run gives 2 m/s.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: slope: Vertical change divided by horizontal change. Requires units and a chosen interval.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Equal distances added in equal times.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: 2 m each second gives a straight rising line.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: constant speed: Equal distances added in equal times. A horizontal line represents zero speed.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Total distance from detecting a hazard to a complete stop.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: 20 m reaction plus 28 m braking = 48 m.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: stopping distance: Total distance from detecting a hazard to a complete stop. Not just braking distance.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Distance travelled while brakes slow the vehicle.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: The car moves 28 m after brakes engage.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: braking distance: Distance travelled while brakes slow the vehicle. Excludes the earlier reaction interval.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Space or time gap behind a vehicle ahead.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: A longer gap gives more room in rain.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: following distance: Space or time gap behind a vehicle ahead. It is not the stopping distance itself.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Decrease in velocity over time.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: Braking reduces speed each second.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: deceleration: Decrease in velocity over time. Its magnitude depends on conditions.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Product of mass and velocity.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: momentum: Product of mass and velocity. Direction follows velocity.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Amount of matter used in this model, measured in kilograms.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: A 750 kg car has more mass than a 70 kg cyclist.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: mass: Amount of matter used in this model, measured in kilograms. Not the same as force.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Velocity assigned positive or negative according to a chosen direction.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: 20 m/s east can be +20 m/s.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: signed velocity: Velocity assigned positive or negative according to a chosen direction. The sign is a direction convention, not speed itself.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Combined external force that changes an object’s motion.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: Braking friction changes vehicle momentum.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: net force: Combined external force that changes an object’s motion. Not identical to momentum.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Force opposing relative motion between contacting surfaces.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: Tire-road grip helps a vehicle decelerate.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: friction: Force opposing relative motion between contacting surfaces. Friction is a force, not momentum.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Using a system to produce forces that slow motion.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: Brakes help tires apply slowing forces to a road.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: braking: Using a system to produce forces that slow motion. The vehicle still moves while slowing.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Average net force multiplied by its action time; equal to momentum change.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: 100 N for 2 s gives 200 N·s.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: impulse: Average net force multiplied by its action time; equal to momentum change. Not the same as momentum itself.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Duration over which interacting objects exert force.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: A glove stops a ball over 0.30 s.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: contact time: Duration over which interacting objects exert force. Longer time alone is meaningful only with context.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Final momentum minus initial momentum.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: A +6 kg·m/s cart stopping has Δp = −6 kg·m/s.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: change in momentum: Final momentum minus initial momentum. Can be negative in a chosen direction.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Momentum change divided by the interaction time.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: 10,000 kg·m/s over 2 s gives 5000 N magnitude.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: average force: Momentum change divided by the interaction time. Instantaneous peak force may differ.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Duration over which motion changes to a stop.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: A cushion may lengthen the stop to 0.75 s.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: stopping time: Duration over which motion changes to a stop. Not the same as reaction time.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Change in shape during a force or impact.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: A crushable front structure folds during impact.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: deformation: Change in shape during a force or impact. Not every deformation improves safety.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Total momentum stays constant for a system with negligible external impulse.

fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: conservation of momentum: Total momentum stays constant for a system with negligible external impulse. Individual momenta may change.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Objects chosen together for an analysis.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: Both colliding carts form one system.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: system: Objects chosen together for an analysis. A different boundary changes external-force accounting.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Momentum change caused by forces from outside the chosen system.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: Road friction acts on the car pair from outside.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: external impulse: Momentum change caused by forces from outside the chosen system. Cannot be ignored automatically.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Momentum assigned positive or negative by direction.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: Right +6 and left −6 sum to zero.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: signed momentum: Momentum assigned positive or negative by direction. Signs are not damage ratings.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Vehicle area designed to deform in some impacts.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: The front structure folds during a crash test.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: crumple zone: Vehicle area designed to deform in some impacts. Not a guarantee against injury.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Cabin structure designed to preserve space.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: The passenger compartment resists crushing.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: rigid occupant cell: Cabin structure designed to preserve space. Different job from a crumple zone.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Feature supporting vehicle use and awareness.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: Mirrors help show surrounding traffic.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: operational feature: Feature supporting vehicle use and awareness. Not primarily an energy absorber.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Roadside structure that can redirect or contain a vehicle.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: A divider separates opposing lanes.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: road barrier: Roadside structure that can redirect or contain a vehicle. Effect depends on design and site.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Restraint with lap and shoulder portions.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: A lap-and-shoulder belt spreads restraint load.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: three-point belt: Restraint with lap and shoulder portions. Fit and placement still matter.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Mechanism that manages belt webbing and locks under specified conditions.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: A belt can extend normally then lock in a rapid event.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: retractor: Mechanism that manages belt webbing and locks under specified conditions. Specific mechanisms vary.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Child restraint installed with child facing the rear of the vehicle.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: The seat shell supports head, neck and back.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: rear-facing seat: Child restraint installed with child facing the rear of the vehicle. Use current size and installation guidance.

fill-in-the-blanks.prompt: Name the term: Rapidly inflating supplemental restraint for specified impacts.
fill-in-the-blanks.hint: An airbag works with a seat belt.
fill-in-the-blanks.explanation: airbag: Rapidly inflating supplemental restraint for specified impacts. Not a replacement for a belt.

s24-d-required-01.title: Reaction time, road risk and injury · required check

questions.prompt: A hazard is 35 m away. A vehicle goes 20 m/s and reaction takes 1 s. What is known?

questions.explanation: The reaction calculation alone cannot establish a complete stop.

options.text: It travels 20 m before braking; 15 m remains but stopping is not proven.
The remaining 15 m is its braking distance.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly separates injury and risk?
questions.hint: Name the quantity, mechanism or assumption before choosing.
questions.explanation: The terms describe different parts of a safety claim.

options.text: Risk describes a chance; injury is a possible outcome.
An injury statistic is a personal prediction.

writing.prompt: A cyclist enters a crossing 30 m ahead of a vehicle moving at 15 m/s. The driver takes 1.2 s to react. Calculate reaction distance and explain what you still need to know before claiming the vehicle will stop in time. Explain your method and name an assumption.

questions.prompt: Two people consume the same stated number of drinks. What can you infer?

options.text: The count alone is insufficient to determine identical BAC or ability.

questions.prompt: A tired driver feels more awake after coffee. Which conclusion follows?

questions.explanation: Subjective alertness is not a complete performance test.

An automobile collision is much more serious than falling off a bicycle or down

Reaction Time
A Need for Safety• MHR 237
The time it takes you to recognize a problem and act  
on it is called reaction time . In the chapter opener,  
you were unable to stop because you had not been 
paying 
attention. Let’s rewind the situation from the 
chapter opener. Pretend that you did not lean down to 
adjust the radio station. Could you have stopped in 
time?
Even if you are alert and react very quickly, there are
many factors that affect a driver’s ability to stop. The
road may have been icy. Your car might have had bald
tires or poor brakes. As a result, you might have slid
into the car in front of you even though you had been
paying attention.
Some drivers have a habit of following too closely.
These drivers do not always have enough room to stop
if the car in front stops suddenly. Look at figure 13.2.
What could happen to the second car if one of the
horses bolts and runs across the road in front of the
first car? What else might happen?
Reaction Time and Distractions
Anything that takes your attention away from what you 
are supposed to be doing is called a distraction. You 
cannot really stop distractions from occurring outside 
your car. However, you can control the distractions 
inside your vehicle.
Are cellular phones really a problem? Statistics 
suggest they are. Dialling or having a conversation on a 
cell phone can slow reaction time. During some 
conversations, reaction time can be slowed by up to three 
times. For example, a driver who usually reacts in two 
seconds may take six seconds to react. This is why many 
provinces have laws banning use of a cellular phone while 
driving.

can be very distracting. What traffic law(s) relate to

might slow reaction time.

Fatigue and Reaction Time
Fifteen percent of drivers surveyed said they have
actually fallen asleep while driving! Sleepy drivers are
a serious danger to themselves and others because
they cannot pay enough attention to the road and
traffic demands. Like drunk drivers, they may
• run off the road;
• roll their vehicle into a ditch; or
• cross the centre line and drive into oncoming
traffic, possibly killing other people and themselves.
Some people think they can drink coffee to stay 
awake, because coffee contains caffeine, which is a 
stimulant. Stimulants increase heart rate and speed 
up reaction 
time. However, when the effects wear off, 
the user 
is more tired than before — and therefore 
has a slower reaction time.
No amount of caffeine, loud music, cold air, or pinching yourself will keep you
awake. Sleep is the only cure. Pull over to a safe parking place and take a nap.
Reaction Time and Drugs
This morning, you woke up feeling sick, so you took a cold remedy before  
coming to school. Y our nose is not running any more, but your head feels 
woozy. Believe it or not, you are impaired . This means you are unable to  
function normally. Alcohol, prescription drugs, and n on-prescription drugs  
can affect the human body in ways that make it dangerous for a user to drive.
Alcohol is absorbed from the stomach and the small intestine directly into the
bloodstream. The human body recognizes alcohol as a poison. The liver produces
enzymes that change it into other, safer chemicals. However, once someone has
consumed one drink, there is too much alcohol for the liver to deal with all of it
at once. The alcohol will move through the blood and have toxic effects.
Alcohol is a depressant. This means that it slows reactions, 
lowers 
co-ordination, and makes the drinker sleepy when it 
reaches the brain tissue.
240 MHR • Safety in Transportation
Figure 13.4 Driving when you are tired can be deadly because
fatigue slows reaction time. If you find yourself yawning or
blinking, pull over in a safe place and have a nap.
Statistics show that many teenagers die while driving
at night and with their friends in the car. For this
reason, many provinces now have a multi-step driver’s
licence policy. First you get your learner’s licence — you can drive only when you
have another, experienced driver in the car with you. Second, you get a licence
that allows you to drive under certain restrictions. For example, you might be
allowed to drive only during the day or with a certain number of passengers.
In provinces where this graduated licencing system is used, inexperienced
drivers have been getting into fewer accidents.

Blood Alcohol Concentration
H ow do people know whether or not they have had too much alcohol and should 
not drive? Courts can use a BAC (blood alcohol concentration) reading. BAC  
refers to the number of milligrams of alcohol in a millilitre of blood. If a 
person’s BAC is 0.08, this means that there are 0.08 mg of alcohol in each mL 
of the person’s
 blood.
Each individual’s BAC depends on the
number of drinks consumed and body
weight. One drink is defined as 45 mL of
hard liquor (40%), 150 mL of wine (11%),
or 350 mL of beer (4%).
How much any individual can drink 
depends on 
body weight. Two drinks, one 
after the other, will put anyone weighing 
45 k
g or less over the legal limit. A person 
who weighs 110 kg may be able to have 
four or five drinks, one after the other, 
before reaching the 
legal limit.
BAC does not take into account the
amount of food or sleep that a person has
had, or the rate at which a person drinks.
Generally, having one drink per hour at a
party is considered safe for driving. But someone who is
tired or hungry can become impaired much more quickly.
BAC also does not take years of drinking experience
into account. An older, heavy drinker may have a BAC
of 0.8 (10 times higher than the legal limit) and not
show any signs of impairment. A younger or smaller
person can often have a BAC well below the legal
limit and be too impaired to drive safely.
Blood Alcohol and the Law
What does the law say about drinking and 
driving? In Canada, a BAC level of 0.08 is 
generally considered the legal limit. However, 
a police officer can charge drivers who have 
any alcohol on their breath when they are  
pulled over. The charge is impaired driving.
Drivers are considered to be impaired
when their reactions are slower than normal.
This includes slurred or slow speech and
being unable to walk in a straight line.

before the crash.
Many bars now offer devices that test BAC, so that drinkers can test
their alcohol levels before they walk out the door. A BAC level is not
the only or the best measure of impairment. People who feel dizzy,
giggly, wobbly, or at all unsure of their abilities, should not drive. It is
better for such people to stay where they are, and start drinking water
or soft drinks instead of alcohol. Many bars also provide free non-
alcoholic drinks to designated drivers.

Collision Injuries
A Need for Safety • MHR 243
13.3
Collisions cause damage to more than cars. People involved in a
rear-end accident like the one described in the chapter opener
may have serious physical injuries. Some may also have emotional
problems as a result of the accident.
The physical and emotional stress that results from an accident 
is referred 
to as trauma . Physical trauma can range from cuts and 
scrapes to 
more serious and lasting injuries like broken bones, 
w hiplash, and brain damage.
Some of these injuries heal on their own, while others do not.
Physical therapy or Chiropratic care may help to correct some
damage. Some injuries cannot be repaired. These include injuries
that involve major brain damage, require amputation, or involve
the spinal cord.
Physical traumas are often visible. Emotional traumas are not.
Some people may feel fearful of all driving after an accident.

Slowing Momentum
As every cyclist and driver knows, the best way to counteract 
momentum is by braking. Brakes apply a force that stops vehicles by 
decreasing their momentum. 
Brakes work using friction. Friction is the force that two objects 
exert on each other when they press against each other. Braking uses 
friction in two ways:
• Applying the brake pedal activates machinery that presses brake
pads against the inside of brake drums on the vehicle’s wheels.
That is one source of friction that slows momentum.
• There is also friction between the vehicle’s tires and the surface
of the road.  During braking, this friction reduces momentum. 
Brakes work best in dry conditions when the brake machinery is in
good condition. Worn brakes do not work as quickly against
momentum. In addition, roads that are slippery due to rain, ice, or
snow will reduce the amount of friction and therefore slow the speed
of braking. 
Friction also works with canoes and kayaks, in which you can stop
paddling and gradually glide to a stop.

Imagine two vehicles travelling along a road in the same direction. Each has its

Safety engineers continue to improve the safety features of
vehicles. The first generation air bags caused many
problems. After trials, testing, and improvement, the second
generation design worked better. Second generation air bags
deploy at a safer speed, at a safer force (from 20 to 35

the ones that came before. There are now seat sensors that
detect the mass of the occupant and adjust the force of the
air bag accordingly. Some of the new air bags also have
switches so they can be turned off if there is a child in the
front seat.

catcher’s mitt. They change shape to cradle a body that is
thrown against them.

you fly forward.

firmly as you fly back.

correctly, it is possible to come through a serious crash
practically without injury!

Conservation of Momentum
Imagine two vehicles travelling along a road in the same direction. Each has its
own momentum. Since people usually refer to car velocities in km/h, we will
use these units when calculating vehicles’ momentum.
Now picture the vehicle behind rear-ending the vehicle in front. What

down because of the impact. It experiences a negative force.

friction is minimal and the vehicles lock together, the total momentum between
the two vehicles does not change. This is also true if one vehicle bumps into
another and there is no damage. During such a collision, one vehicle will lose
momentum at the same rate that the other gains it.

Safety Systems Continue to Improve
Safety engineers continue to improve the safety features of
vehicles. The first generation air bags caused many
problems. After trials, testing, and improvement, the second
generation design worked better. Second generation air bags
deploy at a safer speed, at a safer force (from 20 to 35
percent less than the first generation ones), and work with
the seat belt to protect car occupants.

the ones that came before. There are now seat sensors that
detect the mass of the occupant and adjust the force of the
air bag accordingly. Some of the new air bags also have
switches so they can be turned off if there is a child in the
front seat.
Modern seats are now designed to act like a baseball
catcher’s mitt. They change shape to cradle a body that is
thrown against them.

you fly forward.
•Seats and raised headrests should catch you gently but
firmly as you fly back.

correctly, it is possible to come through a serious crash
practically without injury!

s24-d-l09-transfer.title: Stopping time, force and injury · Use the idea in a new way
